title: Pricing by hours per project for Pool and spa servicing
audience: Owners and supervisors of pool and spa servicing businesses who write quotes for chemistry visits, cleans, equipment checks and one-off jobs, and need a price that covers cost and earns a margin.
learningOutcomes: Calculate a cost per productive hour from the owner's own figures
Estimate visit and project hours, including set-up, travel between pools, and checking time
Build a quote from hours, a rate and a margin, and state its basis and exclusions

instruction.heading: Why hours are the starting unit
instruction.body: A pool round is a set of visits joined by driving. The crew's time, the travel between sites, the test kit set-up and the readings all become hours. Once you know the hours, you can see the cost, the margin and the effect of a change in scope, such as adding a filter clean or a spa drain. A flat price with no hours behind it hides both risk and waste, and it is hard to defend when a client asks why a visit costs what it does.

instruction.heading: Build the cost per productive hour
instruction.body: Take the total cost of running the business over a period and divide it by the productive hours in the same period. Total cost includes wages with on-costs such as leave and superannuation, where your staff arrangements require them, vehicle running costs, test kits and chemicals not charged separately, equipment, insurance, administration and premises. Productive hours are the hours spent on chargeable work at the pool, not the paid hours on a roster. Use billable hours as the divisor. For illustration only, if you pay for 40 hours and 30 of them are chargeable, the cost per productive hour is higher than the hourly wage. Business.gov.au says that on-costs such as super and leave belong in the hourly figure (1 October 2026).

instruction.heading: Estimate the hours
instruction.body: Break each visit into tasks: the test and balance, the walls and waterline, the skimmer and basket, the filter, the equipment check and the readings log. Estimate each task at a standard speed, then add set-up, pack-down, travel between sites and a checking allowance. Add a set allowance for delays outside your control, such as access problems, a locked gate, weather or staff absence. Xero Australia suggests adding 10 to 20 percent to job estimates for unexpected work (3 September 2026); use that range as a starting point and size your own allowance from your records. Record the actual hours after each job and note the reason for any gap. Markel Direct's trade-pricing guide also lists every task, including travel and set-up, as the first step, though the research file labels it an Australian guide and its domain suggests a UK publisher, so check that before relying on it for Australian rules.

instruction.heading: Turn hours into a price
instruction.body: Multiply the crew hours by the cost per productive hour to get the cost of the visit or project. Add a margin that reflects your target and the risk, such as a difficult pump room, a neglected pool or a tight deadline. Apply your chemicals policy and your minimum charge. Where a pool must be drained to sewer, the discharge time can be a large part of the job. Unitywater's policy in Queensland limits sewer discharge to 0.5 litres a second within set hours, so the time must be a named line in the quote. Where the policy does not apply, the time depends on your own pump and the local rules.

instruction.heading: Keep the quote honest
instruction.body: A quote should state the scope, the hours or price basis, the exclusions, what the client must provide, and how long the quote is valid. Exclusions for a pool quote often include repairs, pump or heater replacement, barrier inspections, water supplied by the client, and drainage that needs a licence. Do not show the internal cost per hour to the client unless your policy says to. Business.gov.au says a quote should recover every cost and add a margin. The ACCC says misleading price statements are prohibited (setting prices: what's allowed, 15 July 2026). Re-quote whenever the scope changes.

instruction.heading: Review your estimates
instruction.body: Compare estimated and actual hours for at least the first ten visits or projects of each type. Carters Trade Leader recommends using the gap between quoted and actual labour to correct the next quote (1 October 2025). If the variance stays above a threshold you have agreed, change the standard time, the margin or the scope rules. A pricing method is finished when quoted hours match actual hours closely enough for the work to make money.

procedure: Gather the year's total business costs and the productive hours achieved in the same period.
Divide total costs by productive hours to get the cost per productive hour.
Break each visit into tasks, including the test, the filter, the equipment check and the readings log, and estimate each task time as a range.
Add set-up, pack-down, travel between pools and checking time as named lines.
Multiply total crew hours by the cost per productive hour, then apply the margin for risk and target.
Apply the chemicals policy and the minimum charge, and add any drain or discharge time as a named line.
Write the quote with scope, hours basis, exclusions, client inputs and validity.
Record actual hours after each job and compare them with the estimate.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative figures only, not market rates. A fortnightly residential pool visit takes 1.5 crew-hours on site, including the test and checking, and 0.5 crew-hours of travel between sites. The owner's cost per productive hour is $60 AUD (illustrative). The target margin on price is 25 per cent (illustrative).
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the cost of the visit, what is the price with a 25 per cent margin on price, and what changes if the client asks for a full drain to sewer in an area served by Unitywater?
workedExamples.reasoning: The cost is 2.0 crew-hours multiplied by $60 AUD, which is $120 AUD (illustrative). A 25 per cent margin on price means the price is the cost divided by 0.75, which gives $160 AUD (illustrative). A drain to sewer changes the hours. The Unitywater policy limits sewer discharge to 0.5 litres a second within set hours. A 50,000-litre pool (illustrative size) at that rate would need about 28 hours of pumping (50,000 divided by 0.5 gives 100,000 seconds, or about 27.8 hours). Only the attended hours are crew cost, so the owner must decide, and state in the quote, whether the client pays for unattended pumping time and who checks the discharge.

equipmentAndPpe: Time log for each visit or project, with estimated and actual columns
Pool test kit or digital tester and a readings log

commonErrors.error: Pricing from the hourly wage alone
commonErrors.prevention: Include on-costs, vehicle, equipment, insurance and administration in the cost per productive hour.

commonErrors.error: Counting paid hours as productive hours
commonErrors.prevention: Use chargeable hours only when calculating the cost per productive hour.

commonErrors.error: Leaving out travel between pools, set-up and checking time
commonErrors.prevention: Add these as named lines on every estimate, because a pool round is mostly driving between sites.

commonErrors.error: Quoting a drain or discharge with no time for it
commonErrors.prevention: Check the local discharge rule first, then price the pumping time and any attendance as named lines.

commonErrors.error: Never comparing estimates with actual hours
commonErrors.prevention: Record actual hours after each visit and review the variance monthly.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This is pricing guidance only. The Australian Consumer Law applies to pricing statements, and the ACCC says misleading statements about prices are prohibited. State or territory fair trading rules also apply and differ between states, so check the rules for your state.

Water discharge rules are set by each utility or state. The Unitywater policy (Queensland) and the Icon Water guideline (ACT) are different, and they are the only pool discharge sources found in the research. Neither was checked for other states. Check the rule for the area where you work before you price any drain.

Pay rates, allowances and on-costs for employees may be set by an award or enterprise agreement. Award coverage for pool workers was not checked in this course. Confirm which instrument applies to each worker before using any cost figure.

qualityStandard: Each quote shows scope, hours or price basis, exclusions, client inputs and validity.
The cost per productive hour is calculated from the owner's own records and dated.
Actual hours are recorded for at least the first ten visits or projects of each type and compared with the estimate.
No quote is issued without a margin decision and a minimum-charge check.
documentationEvidence: Cost per productive hour worksheet, dated, with the source of each figure
Quote showing scope, hours basis, exclusions and validity
Visit time log with estimated and actual hours
summary: Hours make the work visible, so start every quote from hours.
Cost per productive hour uses chargeable time, not paid time.
Travel between pools, set-up, checking and any drain time are named lines, not hidden extras.
Compare estimates with actual hours, and change the method when they diverge.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which costs belong in the cost per productive hour for a pool business?
options: Only the hourly wage of the lowest-paid technician and nothing else from the accounts or the rent
The price the client pays, plus the deposit, the late fee and the crew bonus paid
The average hourly rate of other pool businesses in the local area and their fees for the whole year
Wages with on-costs, vehicle, equipment, insurance and administration, divided by chargeable hours

knowledgeChecks.question: A pool visit is estimated at 1.5 crew-hours and takes 2.5. What is the right response?
options: Record the actual hours, find the cause, and adjust the estimate and future quotes
Leave the estimate, since the client has already paid and the crew has finished
Reduce paid hours for the crew on the next job and skip the morning break
Raise the price for this client's next visit only and no one else is charged more

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does a pool quote need an exclusions list?
options: To hide the margin from the client and to keep the rates a secret from the crew
To make the quote longer and to fill up the page with more text and words for the client
To show what the price covers, so scope changes can be priced and disputes are reduced
To lower the client's expectations and to make the job seem much smaller than it is
